> **Continuation of Parts I–II.** We have a Flask inference API, a Streamlit client, Dockerfiles, and a GitHub repository. This article separates four concepts that beginners often mix together: **source hosting, build systems, container registries, and runtime hosting**.

## 1. GitHub is not the same thing as an application server

GitHub is excellent for Git repositories, collaboration and CI/CD. GitHub Pages serves static sites. An ML API needs a Python process somewhere; a Streamlit app also needs a Python process. That “somewhere” is the runtime host.

## 2. Hosting landscape (verify before publishing)

Cloud pricing changes. Treat this table as a snapshot and verify provider pricing when you deploy.

| Platform | Best fit | Free/cheap story | Docker | Main caveat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Streamlit Community Cloud | Streamlit teaching/demo UI | Free public app workflow | Not the main workflow | Streamlit-centric; backend architecture is limited if everything is bundled |
| Render | Beginner-friendly web service/API | Free web services available for hobby/testing | Yes | Free services have limitations and are not for production |
| Railway | Very easy multi-service projects | Free tier/credit, low-cost Hobby | Yes | Usage-based; watch monthly spend |
| Google Cloud Run | Scalable container API/UI | Generous monthly free usage allowance | Yes | Requires cloud project/billing concepts |
| Koyeb | Small container/web service | One constrained free instance; cheap Eco tiers | Yes | Free instance has low CPU/RAM and scales down |
| Hugging Face Spaces | ML demos/community | CPU Basic has no hourly charge, **but new compute Spaces require a paid plan** | Docker supported | No longer universally “free to create” for compute Spaces |

### Important Hugging Face update

Older tutorials often say “Hugging Face Spaces is free.” The current documentation is more nuanced: CPU Basic itself has no hourly charge, but creating a new compute Space (Gradio or Docker) requires a paid plan; static Spaces remain free. That makes it less attractive as the universal zero-cost recommendation it once was.

## 3. Recommendations for this series

For **absolute beginners**, use **Streamlit Community Cloud** when the app can be a single Streamlit process. It is the shortest route from a GitHub repository to a public educational UI.

For the **decoupled Flask + Streamlit architecture**, a strong teaching combination is **Cloud Run for Flask + Streamlit Community Cloud for the UI**. It demonstrates a real API boundary without requiring two always-on servers.

For a **single-provider beginner deployment**, Render is attractive because a Python web service can be connected to a Git repository with little infrastructure work. For a low-cost hobby container, Railway and Koyeb are also worth comparing.

For **scaling concepts**, use Cloud Run: container deployment, scale-to-zero, concurrency, revisions and max-instance controls map naturally to production ideas.

## 4. Render: simple Flask deployment

Add a production command:

```bash
gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:$PORT --workers 2 --threads 2 backend.app:app
```

In Render, create a Web Service from the GitHub repository, select the repository, choose Python or Docker, set the build/start commands, and deploy. If the frontend is a second service, set its `API_URL` environment variable to the backend's public HTTPS URL.

Do not hard-code credentials. Add secrets/environment variables in the provider dashboard.

## 5. Railway: convenient multi-service deployment

A common structure is one Railway project with two services pointing at the same GitHub repository: one service builds `backend/Dockerfile`; the other builds `frontend/Dockerfile`. Give the frontend an `API_URL` variable containing the backend service URL.

Railway is particularly convenient for learners who want less cloud infrastructure vocabulary than a hyperscaler, but the free/paid allowance is usage-based, so teach students to set limits and inspect usage.

## 6. Koyeb: tiny free service or inexpensive Eco compute

Koyeb can deploy a web service from GitHub or a container. Its free instance is appropriate for a small demo, not a serious production API. Because ML libraries can consume substantial RAM, check model size and startup memory before choosing a 512 MB instance.

## 7. Cloud Run: when “scalable” matters

A request-driven serverless container is a good match for stateless inference. Keep the model artifact inside the image for this tutorial. For larger models, use object storage/model registries and deliberately manage startup time and versioning.

A useful cost model is

$$\text{monthly cost}\approx \text{CPU-seconds}\,p_c + \text{GiB-seconds}\,p_m + \text{requests}\,p_r + \text{egress},$$

minus any applicable free-tier allowances. Scale-to-zero is valuable for teaching sites because idle time need not imply an always-running VM.

## 8. What about a VPS?

A small virtual private server can be cheap and predictable, but you become responsible for OS patching, firewall rules, reverse proxy, TLS, process supervision, logs and scaling. It is excellent material **after** students understand managed deployment, not the first deployment path.

## 9. Source-control alternatives to GitHub

If by “alternative to GitHub” you literally mean **where the code repository lives**, GitLab and Bitbucket are mainstream choices. If you mean **where the application runs**, use the runtime hosts above. Keeping these two questions separate prevents a great deal of deployment confusion.

## 10. A decision tree

```text
Do you only need a public Streamlit teaching demo?
 └─ Yes → Streamlit Community Cloud
 └─ No
    Do you want the easiest managed web-service experience?
     └─ Yes → Render / Railway
     └─ No
        Do you want serverless containers + scaling concepts?
         └─ Yes → Google Cloud Run
         └─ No
            Is a tiny hobby service enough?
             └─ Yes → Koyeb free/Eco
             └─ No → paid managed service or VPS/Kubernetes, based on requirements
```

## 11. Dependable deployment means more than “the URL works”

A mature system separates code version, model version and data version; validates inputs; records latency/error metrics; protects secrets; limits abuse; supports rollback; and monitors drift. A deployment tutorial should teach the reader to ask: **What happens when inputs are malformed, traffic doubles, the model changes, or the server restarts?**

## 12. Suggested exercises

1. Add schema validation and return HTTP 422 for invalid feature ranges.
2. Add a `/metrics`-style latency summary without logging personal input data.
3. Compare one large batch request with many single requests and measure latency.
4. Add a second model version and implement a safe rollback.
5. Load-test locally and explain where throughput stops scaling linearly.
6. Deploy the same container to two providers and compare cold-start time and cost.

## Series conclusion

The central lesson is that model deployment is a **systems problem around a statistical object**. The model is only one artifact. A useful ML product also needs a stable feature contract, reproducible preprocessing, an inference interface, a client, environment isolation, source control, runtime infrastructure, observability and a safe update path.
